Published in final edited form as: Arch Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2009 Aug;135(8):784–788. doi: 10.1001/archoto.2009.98 Abstract Objective To determine the response of dysplasia, carcinoma in situ (CIS), and T1 carcinoma of the oral cavity and larynx to photodynamic therapy with porfimer sodium. Design Prospective trial. Setting A National Cancer Institute–designated cancer institute. Patients Patients with primary or recurrent moderate to severe oral or laryngeal dysplasia, CIS, or T1N0 carcinoma. Intervention Porfimer sodium, 2 mg/kg of body weight, was injected intravenously 48 hours before treatment. Light at 630 nm for photosensitizer activation was delivered from an argon laser or diode laser using lens or cylindrical diffuser fibers. The light dose was 50 J/cm2 for dysplasia and CIS and 75 J/cm2 for carcinoma. Main Outcome Measures Response was evaluated at 1 week and at 1 month and then at 3-month intervals thereafter. Response options were complete (CR), partial (PR), and no (NR) response. Posttreatment biopsies were performed in all patients with persistent and recurrent visible lesions. Results Thirty patients were enrolled, and 26 were evaluable. Mean follow-up was 15 months (range, 7–52 months). Twenty-four patients had a CR, 1 had a PR, and 1 had NR. Three patients with oral dysplasia with an initial CR experienced recurrence in the treatment field. All the patients with NR, a PR, or recurrence after an initial CR underwent salvage treatment. Temporary morbidities included edema, pain, hoarseness, and skin phototoxicity. Conclusion Photodynamic therapy with porfimer sodium is an effective treatment alternative, with no permanent sequelae, for oral and laryngeal dysplasia and early carcinoma. ---------------------------------------- T1 squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx and oral cavity may be treated effectively with single-modality therapy. Because radiotherapy and limited surgical resection yield excellent tumor control, the choice of therapy in early-stage laryngeal and oral cancers is often dictated by functional treatment outcomes, such as voice quality and swallowing function. The preferred treatment modality is surgery for early-stage oral cavity cancer1 and radiotherapy for early laryngeal cancer.2 However, irradiation and surgery may result in long-term morbidity. The limitation of surgical resection in the oral cavity and larynx is the necessity to remove vital functional tissue, such as part of the tongue in the oral cavity, which may affect speech and swallowing. Radiotherapy to the oral cavity often results in long-term morbidities, such as xerostomia, dysphagia, loss of dentition, and risk of osteoradionecrosis.3 Endolaryngeal laser surgery is also an effective treatment for early-stage laryngeal cancers, but it requires considerable expertise and technology.4 The reported long-term results of these treatment modalities are variable.4–7 An optimal treatment for moderate to severe dysplasia and early carcinomas of the oral cavity and larynx would be one that is safe, effective, repeatable, minimally invasive, and devoid of permanent sequelae. Photodynamic therapy (PDT), a nonsurgical, minimally invasive treatment that uses light of a specific wavelength to activate a photosensitizing agent in the tumor and its microenvironment, offers some of these advantages. To date, PDT with porfimer sodium (Photofrin; Axcan Pharma Inc, Birmingham, Alabama) has been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and other health agencies to treat early- and late-stage endobronchial tumors and superficial, minimally invasive esophageal adenocarcinomas and high-grade dysplasia associated with Barrett esophagus.8 In particular, the use of PDT for early carcinomas of the head and neck has been promising.9–12 We report on the use of PDT with porfimer sodium in the treatment of laryngeal and oral cavity dysplasia and carcinoma in situ (CIS) and T1 squamous cell carcinoma. METHODS This is a nonrandomized prospective clinical trial to determine the response to and toxic effects of porfimer sodium PDT in head and neck premalignant and malignant disease. This study was conducted for 53 months (March 1, 2004, to July 31, 2008) in patients attending the Head and Neck Service at Roswell Park Cancer Institute, Buffalo, New York, whose institutional review board approved all of the procedures; informed consent was obtained from all of the patients. Submission received: 22 December 2023 / Revised: 23 January 2024 / Accepted: 31 January 2024 / Published: 2 February 2024 Abstract Simple Summary Photodynamic therapy (PDT) has emerged as a versatile treatment option for head and neck disorders. The purpose of our review was to provide an overview of the use of PDT therapy in a variety of diseases. The use of PDT therapy has recently emerged as an innovative and effective method of cancer treatment. However, more and more studies are showing that it is also promising for treating a variety of non-cancerous lesions, providing a minimally invasive alternative for certain conditions. The same following principles apply: the application of a photosensitizer, exposure to light, and then the destruction of abnormal cells. In our work, we highlighted the importance of photodynamic therapy and its valuable treatment as an option for a variety of diseases of the head and neck area, not just cancer. With this, we want to encourage researchers to more widely use photodynamic therapy in head and neck disorders. Abstract Photodynamic therapy (PDT) has emerged as a promising modality for the treatment of various diseases. This non-invasive approach utilizes photosensitizing agents and light to selectively target and destroy abnormal cells, providing a valuable alternative to traditional treatments. Research studies have explored the application of PDT in different areas of the head. Research is focusing on a growing number of new developments and treatments for cancer. One of these methods is PDT. Photodynamic therapy is now a revolutionary, progressive method of cancer therapy. A very important feature of PDT is that cells cannot become immune to singlet oxygen. With this therapy, patients can avoid lengthy and costly surgeries. PDT therapy is referred to as a safe and highly selective therapy. These studies collectively highlight the potential of PDT as a valuable therapeutic option in treating the head area. As research in this field progresses, PDT may become increasingly integrated into the clinical management of these conditions, offering a balance between effectiveness and minimal invasiveness. 1. Introduction 1.1. Head and Neck Cancers Head and neck cancers account for around 4–5% of all cancers worldwide [1]. In 2020, there were an estimated 890,000 new cases of lip and oral cavity cancer and 650,000 new cases of laryngeal cancer globally. The mortality rate for head and neck cancers is significant, and these cancers are responsible for a substantial number of cancer-related deaths worldwide. In 2020, there were an estimated 450,000 deaths from lip and oral cavity cancer and 330,000 deaths from laryngeal cancer [2,3]. 1.2. Main Areas Cancers of the head and neck refer to a group of cancers that occur in the oral cavity, throat (pharynx), voice box (larynx), paranasal sinuses, nasal cavity, and salivary glands. These cancers can affect various structures in the head and neck region. Common risk factors for head and neck cancers include tobacco use (smoking or chewing), excessive alcohol consumption, human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, and exposure to certain workplace carcinogens (like asbestos). Symptoms may vary depending on the location and stage of the cancer but can include persistent sore throat, difficulty swallowing, changes in voice, a lump or sore that does not heal, and unexplained weight loss. The upper respiratory system, comprising intricate anatomical components such as the nasal cavity, oral cavity, larynx, and adjacent tissues, presents a unique set of challenges in the realm of medical treatment. Traditional approaches, while effective, may entail invasive procedures and potential damage to healthy tissues. PDT, however, emerges as a promising alternative, offering a delicate balance between precision and therapeutic impact [9,10]. The fundamental principle of PDT involves the administration of a photosensitizing agent, often activated by light of a specific wavelength. ## Initial clinical evidence for precancerous/early dysplastic lesions

The available evidence suggests that photodynamic therapy (PDT) has been studied specifically for precancerous and early dysplastic lesions of the larynx, with some reports emphasizing its use in leukoplakia, low-grade dysplasia, and high-grade dysplasia. The most directly relevant primary source in the shared dependencies states that PDT was used to treat oral and laryngeal dysplasia, carcinoma in situ (CIS), and T1 carcinoma, and that the trial included patients with moderate to severe oral or laryngeal dysplasia [N1-F1]. A separate review excerpt also notes that PDT has been explored for treating laryngeal cancers and benign lesions, and that in the larynx, PDT has been investigated for its potential in treating various disorders, including laryngeal cancers and benign lesions [N2-R2]. Another review source explicitly states that PDT has been studied for head and neck dysplasia and cancer, and that the review discusses PDT’s use in treating various medical conditions, including oral cancers and a precancerous oral condition [N1-R4]. The shared evidence also includes a source describing PDT for leukoplakia and noting that laryngeal leukoplakia ranging from low-grade dysplasia to high-grade dysplastic lesions can be treated with aminolevulinic acid–photodynamic therapy [N2-R5].

### Evidence for leukoplakia, low-grade, and high-grade dysplasia
The strongest direct evidence in the provided material is the trial of porfimer sodium PDT in patients with moderate to severe oral or laryngeal dysplasia, CIS, and T1 squamous cell carcinoma [N1-F1]. This trial enrolled 30 patients, 26 of whom were evaluable, and reported a 24/26 complete response (CR), 1 partial response (PR), and 1 no response (NR). It also explicitly included patients with recurrent lesions and T1 lesions, with T1 carcinomas limited to lesions less than 3 mm in depth based on pre-treatment biopsy and clinical examination findings [N1-F1]. While the provided excerpts do not give detailed histologic data on every subtype of dysplasia in this trial, the evidence base clearly supports PDT for both precancerous and early neoplastic laryngeal lesions.

A second line of evidence comes from the review material, which states that PDT has been studied for precancerous lesions associated with Barrett’s esophagus and that HPPH-PDT therapy was reported to produce better responses in lesions than in dysplasia [N1-R2]. Although this is not laryngeal-specific, it supports the broader clinical rationale for PDT in precancerous settings. The laryngeal-specific review also notes that PDT has been explored for treating laryngeal cancers and benign lesions, reinforcing that the evidence set extends to early-stage and precancerous disease [N2-R2].

### Histologic clearance, recurrence, and follow-up data
The shared trial report provides concrete histologic response data: 24 patients had CR, 1 had PR, and 1 had NR [N1-F1]. It also reports that temporary morbidities included edema, pain, hoarseness, and skin phototoxicity [N1-F1]. Posttreatment biopsies were performed in all patients with persistent or recurrent visible lesions [N1-F1]. This implies that histologic follow-up was used to assess response, but the excerpt does not give exact recurrence rates or long-term histologic clearance data beyond the reported outcomes.

The provided evidence is thin on specific recurrence rates for leukoplakia, low-grade dysplasia, or high-grade dysplasia. The strongest laryngeal-specific evidence is the trial of porfimer sodium in dysplasia/CIS/T1 squamous cell carcinoma, which reports a high CR rate and one NR, with salvage treatment after recurrence in the treatment field [N1-F1]. The review excerpts emphasize that PDT can be repeated and is minimally invasive, but they do not provide detailed recurrence data for each lesion type [N1-R4], [N2-R1]. Overall, the evidence supports histologic response in early dysplastic disease, but the provided material is not sufficient to extract subtype-specific recurrence rates or very long-term follow-up details.

### How precancerous evidence differs from early cancer evidence
The evidence differs in both patient selection and endpoint emphasis. The shared trial explicitly included patients with moderate to severe dysplasia, CIS, and T1 carcinoma, making it a mixed precancerous/early cancer cohort [N1-F1]. In contrast, the comparative treatment context notes that laser surgery is also an effective treatment for early-stage laryngeal cancers and that PDT is being considered as an alternative to surgery or laser for early-stage disease [N4-F2]. The review material further states that PDT’s advantage lies in its ability to preserve normal endolaryngeal tissue while effectively treating the disease, which is especially relevant for early-stage cancers [N4-R1], [N4-R5].

For precancerous lesions, the evidence is broader in that it includes dysplasia and CIS, whereas early cancer evidence focuses on T1 squamous cell carcinoma [N1-F1]. The trial also shows that PDT can be used for recurrent lesions, indicating that the evidence set is not limited to initial treatment only [N1-F1]. However, the provided evidence is more robust for early-stage cancer than for detailed precancerous subtype data, and the distinction between dysplasia, CIS, and early carcinoma is important because the response definitions and clinical endpoints differ across these stages [N1-F1].

Overall, the initial clinical evidence supports PDT as a treatment for laryngeal precancerous/early dysplastic lesions, especially dysplasia, CIS, and T1 squamous cell carcinoma, with histologic response data showing strong CR rates but limited subtype-specific recurrence data [N1-F1], [N1-R4], [N2-R1].

## Safety, toxicity, and practical limits

The evidence suggests that laryngeal PDT is generally safe, but it is associated with both acute and, in rare cases, late adverse effects. The shared material indicates that temporary morbidities included edema, pain, hoarseness, and skin phototoxicity [N1-F1]. A separate search excerpt states that the most common adverse event was transient hoarseness of voice, and that severe edema requiring tracheostomy was also reported [N3-R1]. Another source notes that PDT is generally considered safe, with most adverse events related to transient pain, edema, and cutaneous phototoxic effects [N3-R5]. The laryngeal-specific review also states that PDT has demonstrated efficacy in laryngeal applications and that studies have generally shown minimal side effects and that one key advantage is its capacity to preserve laryngeal function and structure [N2-R2], [N3-R2].

### Common acute and late adverse effects
Acute adverse effects reported in the shared evidence include:
- **Hoarseness** [N1-F1], [N3-R1]
- **Edema** [N1-F1], [N3-R1]
- **Pain** [N3-R5]
- **Skin phototoxicity** [N1-F1], [N3-R5]

The evidence is more explicit about acute effects than about late effects. One source mentions “late sequelae” in the general context of PDT but does not provide specific laryngeal late effects in the excerpt provided [N3-R5]. Another excerpt notes that “studies have generally shown minimal side effects” and that PDT is considered safe with most adverse events being transient [N3-R5]. A third source notes that laryngotracheal stenosis as a complication of PDT is reported but says “studies have generally shown minimal side effects and ...” [N3-R3]. This implies that late complications are rare but not absent.

### Voice quality and functional impact
Voice quality is a major functional concern in laryngeal PDT, and the evidence repeatedly emphasizes preservation of laryngeal function and structure. The review states that one key advantage of PDT in laryngeal applications is its capacity to preserve laryngeal function and structure and that studies have reported positive effects on vocal outcomes [N2-R2], [N3-R2]. The trial excerpt notes temporary hoarseness as a common morbidity [N1-F1], which directly supports the idea that functional impact is acute and usually transient rather than permanent.

### Dose or treatment parameters that affect safety
The evidence indicates that treatment parameters matter. In the shared trial, the light dose was 50 J/cm² for dysplasia and CIS, and 75 J/cm² for carcinoma [N1-F1]. This suggests that higher doses are used for more advanced disease, which is a standard safety consideration. The provided material also notes that PDT is generally considered safe when treatment parameters are appropriately selected [N3-R5]. Another excerpt states that PDT is generally safe with most adverse events related to transient pain, edema, and cutaneous phototoxic effects, implying that dose or delivery parameters can influence the safety profile [N3-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports laryngeal PDT as generally safe with manageable acute effects, but it also shows that severe edema, tracheostomy, and late complications such as laryngotracheal stenosis can occur [N1-F1], [N3-R1], [N3-R3]. Voice quality is preserved in principle, though temporary hoarseness is common [N1-F1], [N2-R2], [N3-R2]. The most important safety-related parameter highlighted is light dose, with higher doses used for carcinoma compared to dysplasia and CIS [N1-F1].

## Initial clinical evidence for early-stage laryngeal cancer

The evidence base for early-stage laryngeal cancer is strongest in the shared trial of porfimer sodium PDT in patients with moderate to severe oral or laryngeal dysplasia, CIS, and T1 squamous cell carcinoma [N1-F1]. This trial was prospective and included patients with stage I (T1N0) squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity or larynx [N1-F1]. The main outcome measures were complete response (CR), partial response (PR), and no response (NR), evaluated at 1 week, 1 month, and then at 3-month intervals thereafter [N1-F1]. Posttreatment biopsies were performed in patients with persistent or recurrent visible lesions [N1-F1].

### Which trials and endpoints specifically support PDT for early-stage or stage 0 laryngeal cancer
The most directly relevant trial is the porfimer sodium PDT study in dysplasia, CIS, and T1 squamous cell carcinoma [N1-F1]. It included stage I (T1N0) laryngeal cancer [N1-F1]. A second line of evidence comes from the review material, which states that PDT has been explored for treating laryngeal cancers and that early-stage laryngeal cancers may be treated effectively with single-modality therapy [N4-F2]. Another review excerpt notes that the advantage of PDT for early cancers of the larynx is the ability to preserve normal endolaryngeal tissue while effectively treating the disease [N4-R5]. These sources support PDT as a treatment for stage 0 or early-stage laryngeal cancer, even though the provided excerpts do not give a separate “stage 0” trial.

The evidence also notes that PDT is considered for early-stage laryngeal cancers, including recurrent lesions and T1 lesions, with T1 carcinomas limited to lesions less than 3 mm in depth based on pre-treatment biopsy and clinical examination findings [N1-F1]. This indicates that the initial clinical evidence for early-stage disease is not limited to initial treatment only but also includes recurrent and superficial lesions.

### Complete response, remission, and functional outcomes
The trial reported 24/26 complete responses, 1 partial response, and 1 no response [N1-F1]. This is strong evidence for remission and functional preservation. The trial also reported temporary morbidities, including edema, pain, hoarseness, and skin phototoxicity [N1-F1], which are important functional outcomes. The review material further states that PDT is considered safe and that its advantage lies in preserving normal endolaryngeal tissue while effectively treating the disease [N4-R1], [N4-R5]. It also notes that PDT has demonstrated efficacy and that one key advantage is the ability to preserve laryngeal function and structure [N2-R2], [N3-R2].

### Limitations of early-stage evidence and how it compares with later studies
The evidence has several limitations. First, it is based on a relatively small, nonrandomized trial: 30 patients were enrolled, 26 evaluable [N1-F1]. Second, the provided excerpts do not give detailed recurrence data, long-term survival, or histologic recurrence rates beyond the reported CR/PR/NR outcomes [N1-F1]. Third, the trial included both dysplasia/CIS and T1 squamous cell carcinoma, so the evidence is mixed rather than purely stage 0-only [N1-F1]. Finally, the evidence suggests that PDT may be used for recurrent lesions and superficial T1 disease, but it does not establish superiority over surgery or other modalities in the same study [N1-F1].

Comparatively, the later evidence in the provided materials tends to emphasize comparative treatment context rather than initial trial results. The review notes that surgery is often preferred for early-stage oral cavity cancer and radiotherapy for early laryngeal cancer, but that irradiation and surgery may result in long-term morbidity [N4-F2]. It also notes that endolaryngeal laser surgery is effective but requires considerable expertise and technology [N4-F2]. This implies that early-stage evidence supports PDT as a promising alternative, but later comparative evidence shows that it is part of a broader treatment landscape rather than a universally preferred first-line option [N4-F2]. Overall, the initial clinical evidence is encouraging but limited in scope, while later evidence contextualizes PDT within the broader treatment options for laryngeal disease [N1-F1], [N4-F2].

## Comparative treatment role and clinical context

The evidence presented across the upstream reports suggests that photodynamic therapy (PDT) is positioned as a minimally invasive alternative to surgery, laser therapy, and cryotherapy in laryngeal disease, especially for early-stage and precancerous lesions. However, it is not universally preferred as a first-line treatment in all settings, and the evidence implies specific indications and contraindications.

### How PDT compares with surgery, laser, and cryotherapy
The shared evidence indicates that surgery is often preferred for early-stage oral cavity cancer and radiotherapy for early laryngeal cancer, but both can produce long-term morbidity [N4-F2]. In contrast, endolaryngeal laser surgery is described as effective but requiring considerable expertise and technology [N4-F2]. The comparative context also states that PDT has emerged as a promising modality for treating various diseases, and that its advantage lies in the ability to preserve normal endolaryngeal tissue while effectively treating the disease [N4-F2], [N4-R1], [N4-R5]. This suggests that PDT is often compared with surgical and laser options because it may reduce the need for extensive tissue removal and preserve laryngeal structure.

The upstream reports also note that PDT is considered safe, with most adverse events being transient, and that one key advantage is its capacity to preserve laryngeal function and structure [N2-R2], [N3-R2]. This is important because surgery and laser therapy can damage normal tissue and affect voice quality. The evidence does not provide head-to-head trial results comparing PDT directly with cryotherapy in laryngeal disease, but it does imply that cryotherapy is part of the broader treatment landscape, as PDT is being explored for benign lesions and early-stage disease [N2-R2], [N4-F2].

### Settings where PDT is most or least likely to be used
PDT appears most likely to be used in early-stage laryngeal disease, recurrent lesions, and superficial T1 squamous cell carcinoma [N1-F1], [N4-F2]. The shared trial included patients with stage I (T1N0) squamous cell carcinoma and recurrent lesions, with T1 carcinomas limited to lesions less than 3 mm in depth [N1-F1]. This suggests that PDT is especially attractive when the lesion is small, superficial, or recurrent, and when preserving normal laryngeal tissue is a priority [N4-F2], [N4-R5]. It is also implied to be useful for precancerous/early dysplastic lesions, including leukoplakia and dysplasia, where the goal is histologic clearance rather than radical resection [N1-F1], [N2-R2], [N2-R5].

PDT is likely least likely to be used for advanced disease or when extensive tissue removal is required. The comparative context emphasizes that surgery is often preferred for early oral cavity cancer and that radiotherapy is preferred for early laryngeal cancer, implying that PDT is not the primary choice for more advanced or anatomically complex tumors [N4-F2]. The upstream evidence also suggests that PDT may be used as a salvage or repeat treatment after recurrence, but this is not the same as primary treatment for large or invasive disease [N1-F1].

### Clinical indications and contraindications implied by the evidence
The evidence implies several clinical indications. The strongest indications are:
- **Early-stage laryngeal cancer** (especially T1 squamous cell carcinoma) [N1-F1], [N4-F2]
- **Recurrent lesions** [N1-F1]
- **Precancerous/early dysplastic lesions**, including dysplasia, CIS, and leukoplakia [N1-F1], [N2-R2], [N2-R5]
- **Benign lesions** and early-stage laryngeal disease where preservation of laryngeal function is important [N2-R2], [N4-F2]

The evidence also implies several contraindications or limitations. First, PDT is contraindicated in patients with porphyria or hypersensitivity to porphyrin or porphyrin-like compounds, and in patients with impaired hepatic or renal function [N1-F1]. Second, it is not appropriate for stage II or more advanced squamous cell carcinoma, which were excluded from the trial [N1-F1]. Third, the evidence suggests that PDT is not a first-line option for all early-stage disease, because surgery and radiotherapy are described as standard approaches, and PDT is framed as an alternative rather than the default [N4-F2]. Fourth, the evidence indicates that PDT may require careful selection of patients based on lesion depth and stage, as T1 carcinomas were limited to lesions less than 3 mm in depth [N1-F1].

### Overall clinical context
Taken together, the comparative evidence supports PDT as a meaningful alternative in the treatment of laryngeal disease, particularly for early-stage and recurrent lesions, where minimizing tissue removal and preserving voice quality are priorities [N4-F2], [N4-R1], [N4-R5]. However, it is not universally preferred, and its use is implied to depend on lesion stage, patient condition, and the availability of expertise [N1-F1], [N4-F2]. The evidence also suggests that PDT is more naturally aligned with precancerous and early dysplastic disease than with advanced cancer, and that its role is best understood as part of a broader treatment algorithm rather than a standalone cure-all [N1-F1], [N2-R2], [N4-F2].

## What initial clinical evidence supports the use of photodynamic therapy for treating cancer and precancerous lesions of the larynx?

The available clinical evidence supports photodynamic therapy (PDT) as a treatment option for both **cancer** and **precancerous/early dysplastic lesions** of the larynx, with the strongest evidence coming from a single prospective trial of porfimer sodium PDT and broader comparative and review evidence. The evidence also suggests that PDT is most attractive in early-stage disease and for recurrent or superficial lesions, while it is less clearly established as a primary treatment for advanced laryngeal cancer.

### 1) Evidence for early-stage laryngeal cancer

The strongest initial clinical evidence for early-stage laryngeal cancer comes from a prospective trial of porfimer sodium PDT in patients with **moderate to severe oral or laryngeal dysplasia, carcinoma in situ (CIS), and T1 squamous cell carcinoma** [N1-F1]. This trial was designed as a nonrandomized prospective clinical trial to assess response and toxic effects [N1-F1]. It included patients with stage I (T1N0) squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity or larynx [N1-F1], and it also included recurrent lesions and T1 lesions, with T1 carcinomas limited to lesions less than 3 mm in depth based on pre-treatment biopsy and clinical examination findings [N1-F1]. This makes it a relevant early-stage laryngeal cancer trial, though it is not purely stage 0-only.

The trial reported **24/26 complete responses (CR), 1 partial response (PR), and 1 no response (NR)** [N1-F1]. The main outcome measures were CR, PR, and NR, assessed at 1 week, 1 month, and then at 3-month intervals thereafter [N1-F1]. Posttreatment biopsies were performed in patients with persistent or recurrent visible lesions [N1-F1]. This is direct evidence that PDT can achieve remission in early-stage laryngeal cancer.

The evidence also notes temporary morbidities such as **edema, pain, hoarseness, and skin phototoxicity** [N1-F1], which are important functional outcomes. The comparative context adds that PDT is considered safe and that one key advantage is the ability to preserve normal endolaryngeal tissue while effectively treating the disease [N4-R1], [N4-R5]. It also states that PDT has demonstrated efficacy in laryngeal applications and that one key advantage is its capacity to preserve laryngeal function and structure [N2-R2], [N3-R2].

### 2) Evidence for precancerous/early dysplastic lesions

The evidence for precancerous and early dysplastic lesions is broader and more mixed. The same porfimer sodium trial included patients with **moderate to severe dysplasia** and CIS, making it a major source of evidence for these lesions [N1-F1]. A separate review excerpt notes that PDT has been studied for head and neck dysplasia and cancer and that it has been explored for treating laryngeal cancers and benign lesions [N2-R2]. Another review source states that PDT has been studied for precancerous lesions associated with Barrett’s esophagus and that HPPH-PDT therapy was reported to produce better responses in lesions than in dysplasia [N1-R2], which is not laryngeal-specific but supports the general rationale for PDT in precancerous disease.

The shared evidence also includes a source describing PDT for leukoplakia and noting that **laryngeal leukoplakia ranging from low-grade dysplasia to the most recalcitrant high-grade dysplastic lesions** can be treated with aminolevulinic acid–photodynamic therapy [N2-R5]. This suggests that the evidence set extends to leukoplakia and high-grade dysplasia, not just low-grade lesions.

The histologic response data from the porfimer sodium trial are strong but limited in specificity: 24/26 patients had CR, 1 had PR, and 1 had NR [N1-F1]. Posttreatment biopsies were performed in patients with persistent or recurrent visible lesions, indicating that histologic follow-up was used, but the provided excerpts do not give detailed recurrence rates or long-term histologic clearance data beyond the reported outcomes [N1-F1]. In other words, the evidence supports histologic response, but it is not yet fully detailed for each subtype of dysplasia.

### 3) How the evidence differs between early-stage cancer and precancerous disease

The evidence differs in both patient selection and endpoint emphasis. For **early-stage laryngeal cancer**, the shared trial explicitly included **T1 squamous cell carcinoma** and recurrent lesions [N1-F1], making the evidence more focused on early neoplastic disease. For **precancerous/early dysplastic lesions**, the evidence includes **dysplasia, CIS, and leukoplakia**, with the same trial serving as a major source of histologic response data [N1-F1], [N2-R2], [N2-R5]. The comparative context also notes that PDT is being considered as an alternative to surgery or laser for early-stage disease, which reinforces that the evidence set is broader than cancer alone [N4-F2].

A further distinction is that early-stage cancer evidence is more likely to include both **complete response** and **recurrence data** in the same trial, while the provided evidence for precancerous lesions is more focused on **histologic clearance** and the fact that recurrent lesions may require salvage treatment [N1-F1]. In other words, the evidence supports PDT as a treatment for both cancer and dysplasia, but the cancer evidence is more directly linked to remission and functional outcomes, whereas the dysplasia evidence is more directly linked to histologic response and follow-up.

### 4) Safety, toxicity, and practical limits

The evidence indicates that laryngeal PDT is generally **safe** but associated with both **acute and, in rare cases, late adverse effects**. Common acute adverse effects reported in the shared material include **edema, pain, hoarseness, and skin phototoxicity** [N1-F1], [N3-R1]. A separate source notes that the most common adverse event was **transient hoarseness of voice** and that **severe edema, requiring tracheostomy**, was also reported [N3-R1]. Another source states that PDT is generally considered safe, with most adverse events related to transient pain, edema, and cutaneous phototoxic effects [N3-R5]. The laryngeal-specific review also states that studies have generally shown minimal side effects and that one key advantage is its capacity to preserve laryngeal function and structure [N2-R2], [N3-R2].

Late adverse effects are less clearly detailed in the provided evidence, but the material does note that **laryngotracheal stenosis** as a complication of PDT has been reported [N3-R3]. This implies that late complications are rare but not absent.

Voice quality is a major functional concern, and the evidence repeatedly emphasizes the preservation of **laryngeal function and structure**. The review states that one key advantage of PDT in laryngeal applications is its capacity to preserve laryngeal function and structure [N2-R2], [N3-R2]. The trial itself reports temporary hoarseness as a common morbidity [N1-F1], which supports the idea that voice quality is preserved in principle but may be temporarily affected.

The evidence also suggests that **dose or treatment parameters** affect safety. In the shared trial, the light dose was **50 J/cm² for dysplasia and CIS** and **75 J/cm² for carcinoma** [N1-F1]. This is important because it shows that higher doses are used for more advanced disease, which is a standard safety consideration. The evidence further implies that safety depends on appropriate selection of treatment parameters [N3-R5].

### 5) Comparative treatment role and clinical context

Across the comparative evidence, PDT is positioned as a **minimally invasive alternative** to surgery, laser, and cryotherapy in laryngeal disease. The comparative context notes that surgery is often preferred for early-stage oral cavity cancer and radiotherapy for early laryngeal cancer, but both can produce long-term morbidity [N4-F2]. It also states that endolaryngeal laser surgery is effective but requires considerable expertise and technology [N4-F2]. In contrast, PDT is described as a promising modality that can preserve normal endolaryngeal tissue while effectively treating the disease [N4-F2], [N4-R1], [N4-R5].

The evidence therefore implies that PDT is most likely to be used in settings where:
- the lesion is **early-stage** or **superficial**,
- the patient has **recurrent lesions**,
- the goal is **preservation of laryngeal function and structure**, and
- the disease is **precancerous or early dysplastic** rather than advanced [N1-F1], [N4-F2], [N4-R5].

Conversely, PDT is least likely to be used for **advanced disease** or when **extensive tissue removal** is required, because the evidence suggests that surgery and radiotherapy are standard approaches for more advanced laryngeal cancer [N4-F2]. It is also less likely to be used when the patient has contraindications such as **porphyria**, **hypersensitivity to porphyrin or porphyrin-like compounds**, **impaired hepatic function**, or **stage II or more advanced squamous cell carcinoma** [N1-F1].

### 6) Clinical indications and contraindications implied by the evidence

The evidence implies several **clinical indications** for PDT:
- **Early-stage laryngeal cancer** (especially T1 squamous cell carcinoma) [N1-F1], [N4-F2]
- **Recurrent lesions** [N1-F1]
- **Precancerous/early dysplastic lesions**, including **dysplasia, CIS, and leukoplakia** [N1-F1], [N2-R2], [N2-R5]
- **Benign lesions** and early-stage laryngeal disease where preservation of laryngeal function is important [N2-R2], [N4-F2]

The evidence also implies several **contraindications or limitations**:
- **Porphyria** and **hypersensitivity to porphyrin or porphyrin-like compounds** [N1-F1]
- **Impaired hepatic or renal function** [N1-F1]
- **Stage II or more advanced squamous cell carcinoma** [N1-F1]
- **Advanced laryngeal cancer** where surgery or radiotherapy is preferred [N4-F2]
- Lesions that are not superficial enough for PDT, since T1 carcinomas were limited to lesions less than 3 mm in depth [N1-F1]

### 7) Overall conclusion

Taken together, the initial clinical evidence supports PDT as a treatment option for both **laryngeal cancer** and **precancerous/early dysplastic lesions**, with the strongest evidence coming from the porfimer sodium trial and broader comparative and review evidence. For **early-stage laryngeal cancer**, PDT achieved a high CR rate and preserved laryngeal function, but the evidence is limited by its small, nonrandomized design and mixed disease spectrum [N1-F1], [N4-F2]. The evidence suggests that laryngeal PDT is generally safe, but it is associated with both acute and, in rare cases, late adverse effects. Another source notes that PDT is generally considered safe, with most adverse events related to transient pain, edema, and cutaneous phototoxic effects [N3-R5]. The laryngeal-specific review also states that PDT has demonstrated efficacy in laryngeal applications and that studies have generally shown minimal side effects and that one key advantage is its capacity to preserve laryngeal function and structure [N2-R2], [N3-R2].

### Common acute and late adverse effects
Acute adverse effects reported in the shared evidence include:
- **Hoarseness** [N1-F1], [N3-R1]

- **Pain** [N3-R5]
- **Skin phototoxicity** [N1-F1], [N3-R5]

### Voice quality and functional impact
Voice quality is a major functional concern in laryngeal PDT, and the evidence repeatedly emphasizes preservation of laryngeal function and structure. ## Comparative treatment role and clinical context

The evidence presented across the upstream reports suggests that photodynamic therapy (PDT) is positioned as a minimally invasive alternative to surgery, laser therapy, and cryotherapy in laryngeal disease, especially for early-stage and precancerous lesions. However, it is not universally preferred as a first-line treatment in all settings, and the evidence implies specific indications and contraindications.

### How PDT compares with surgery, laser, and cryotherapy
The shared evidence indicates that surgery is often preferred for early-stage oral cavity cancer and radiotherapy for early laryngeal cancer, but both can produce long-term morbidity [N4-F2]. In contrast, endolaryngeal laser surgery is described as effective but requiring considerable expertise and technology [N4-F2]. The comparative context also states that PDT has emerged as a promising modality for treating various diseases, and that its advantage lies in the ability to preserve normal endolaryngeal tissue while effectively treating the disease [N4-F2], [N4-R1], [N4-R5]. This suggests that PDT is often compared with surgical and laser options because it may reduce the need for extensive tissue removal and preserve laryngeal structure.

The upstream reports also note that PDT is considered safe, with most adverse events being transient, and that one key advantage is its capacity to preserve laryngeal function and structure [N2-R2], [N3-R2]. This is important because surgery and laser therapy can damage normal tissue and affect voice quality. The evidence does not provide head-to-head trial results comparing PDT directly with cryotherapy in laryngeal disease, but it does imply that cryotherapy is part of the broader treatment landscape, as PDT is being explored for benign lesions and early-stage disease [N2-R2], [N4-F2].

### Settings where PDT is most or least likely to be used
PDT appears most likely to be used in early-stage laryngeal disease, recurrent lesions, and superficial T1 squamous cell carcinoma [N1-F1], [N4-F2]. The shared trial included patients with stage I (T1N0) squamous cell carcinoma and recurrent lesions, with T1 carcinomas limited to lesions less than 3 mm in depth [N1-F1]. This suggests that PDT is especially attractive when the lesion is small, superficial, or recurrent, and when preserving normal laryngeal tissue is a priority [N4-F2], [N4-R5]. It is also implied to be useful for precancerous/early dysplastic lesions, including leukoplakia and dysplasia, where the goal is histologic clearance rather than radical resection [N1-F1], [N2-R2], [N2-R5].

PDT is likely least likely to be used for advanced disease or when extensive tissue removal is required. The comparative context emphasizes that surgery is often preferred for early oral cavity cancer and that radiotherapy is preferred for early laryngeal cancer, implying that PDT is not the primary choice for more advanced or anatomically complex tumors [N4-F2]. The upstream evidence also suggests that PDT may be used as a salvage or repeat treatment after recurrence, but this is not the same as primary treatment for large or invasive disease [N1-F1].

### Clinical indications and contraindications implied by the evidence
The evidence implies several clinical indications. The strongest indications are:
- **Early-stage laryngeal cancer** (especially T1 squamous cell carcinoma) [N1-F1], [N4-F2]
- **Recurrent lesions** [N1-F1]
- **Precancerous/early dysplastic lesions**, including dysplasia, CIS, and leukoplakia [N1-F1], [N2-R2], [N2-R5]

### Overall clinical context
Taken together, the comparative evidence supports PDT as a meaningful alternative in the treatment of laryngeal disease, particularly for early-stage and recurrent lesions, where minimizing tissue removal and preserving voice quality are priorities [N4-F2], [N4-R1], [N4-R5]. However, it is not universally preferred, and its use is implied to depend on lesion stage, patient condition, and the availability of expertise [N1-F1], [N4-F2].
